[{"order":1,"type":"heading","text":"Mastering Caching Strategies in System Design"},{"order":2,"type":"paragraph","text":"Caching is a fundamental technique used in distributed systems to reduce latency, decrease database load, and improve overall throughput. Choosing the right caching strategy depends heavily on your application\'s read and write patterns, consistency requirements, and tolerance for data loss."},{"order":3,"type":"subheading","text":"1. Cache-Aside (Lazy Loading)"},{"order":4,"type":"paragraph","text":"In the Cache-Aside pattern, the application is responsible for communicating with both the database and the cache. The cache does not interact with the database directly. When the application needs data, it checks the cache first."},{"order":5,"type":"bullet_point","text":"Read Path: Application checks cache. If hit, return data. If miss, query database, store result in cache, and return data."},{"order":6,"type":"bullet_point","text":"Write Path: Application writes data directly to the database and either invalidates the cache entry or updates it."},{"order":7,"type":"code","text":"def get_user(user_id):
    user = cache.get(user_id)
    if user is None:
        user = db.query("SELECT * FROM users WHERE id = ?", user_id)
        cache.set(user_id, user)
    return user"},{"order":8,"type":"subheading","text":"2. Write-Through"},{"order":9,"type":"paragraph","text":"In the Write-Through strategy, data is written to the cache and the database simultaneously. The cache acts as the primary entry point for writes. The application sends data to the cache, and the cache handles writing it to the underlying database before confirming success to the application."},{"order":10,"type":"bullet_point","text":"Pros: Ensures data in the cache is always fresh and consistent with the database."},{"order":11,"type":"bullet_point","text":"Cons: Higher write latency because every write operation goes to two distinct storage layers."},{"order":12,"type":"subheading","text":"3. Write-Behind (Write-Back)"},{"order":13,"type":"paragraph","text":"With Write-Behind, the application writes data exclusively to the cache. The cache then asynchronously writes the data to the database after a specified delay or when a batch threshold is reached. This pattern provides exceptional write performance."},{"order":14,"type":"bullet_point","text":"Pros: Extremely low write latency and reduces database write operations through batching."},{"order":15,"type":"bullet_point","text":"Cons: Risk of data loss if the cache node crashes before flushing data to the persistent database."},{"order":16,"type":"subheading","text":"4. Refresh-Ahead"},{"order":17,"type":"paragraph","text":"The Refresh-Ahead pattern involves the cache automatically refreshing frequently accessed data before its expiration time arrives. The system predicts access patterns and updates the cache proactively to prevent cache misses on hot data items."},{"order":18,"type":"bullet_point","text":"Pros: Eliminates latency spikes caused by sudden cache expirations for heavy read workloads."},{"order":19,"type":"bullet_point","text":"Cons: Wastes computing resources if data is refreshed but never subsequently read by clients."},{"order":20,"type":"subheading","text":"Summary & Selection Criteria"},{"order":21,"type":"bullet_point","text":"Use Cache-Aside for read-heavy workloads where tolerable staleness is acceptable."},{"order":22,"type":"bullet_point","text":"Use Write-Through when data consistency is critical and write latency can be slightly compromised."},{"order":23,"type":"bullet_point","text":"Use Write-Behind for write-heavy systems where throughput and low latency trump immediate persistence."},{"order":24,"type":"bullet_point","text":"Use Refresh-Ahead for predictable hot-spot data streams requiring strict SLA guarantees."}]
